evals.prompt:
I run `corvane/corvane-action`, our official GitHub Action (JavaScript, node20, currently v2.3.1, about 900 repos on `@v2`). Here's the changelog for 2.4.0 we're cutting Thursday as a minor:

- rename input `api_key` to `api-key` (kebab-case, three customers asked)
- `severity-threshold` default moves from `high` to `medium`, product wants more findings surfaced
- `license-findings` currently warns; it now fails the step like the other finding types
- `runs.using: node24`, the deprecation banners are everywhere
- bundled corvane CLI goes 4.x to 5.0 (5.0 dropped `--format table`, which we never called)
- drop the `verbose` input, telemetry says nobody sets it
- new `output-file` input, default empty

Then we cut the release and move the `v2` tag as usual. Check the plan.
evals.expected_output: An audit of each changelog line against the contract rules and breaking-change table: six of the seven items are majors, bundled into one v3.0.0 whose runtime bump also deletes deprecated inputs, with api_key kept as a deprecated alias through the deprecation sequence, v2 kept patched for GHES, every fix shipped as an immutable vX.Y.Z release rather than a moved tag, release notes carrying the SHA-pinned uses line, and a contract-diff check added to CI.
expectations: Audits the changelog against the contract rules block before discussing any individual item.
Classifies the `api_key` to `api-key` rename as a major, not a minor, because every v2 workflow still sending `api_key` is silently ignored and runs with no key.

Prescribes the deprecation sequence for the rename: add `api-key`, keep `api_key` working and mapped to the same behaviour, set `deprecationMessage` on `api_key`, state the removal major in release notes and README, delete it only in the next major.
Classifies changing the `severity-threshold` default from `high` to `medium` as a major because pinned workflows change behaviour without any edit on the customer side.
Classifies turning the `license-findings` warning into a failure by default as a major because green pipelines go red with no change on the customer side.
Classifies `runs.using: node24` as a major because it raises the minimum runner and excludes GHES releases and self-hosted runners without Node 24, rejecting the 'runtime detail' framing.
Classifies the bundled CLI bump from 4.x to 5.0 with a removed flag as a major per the breaking-change table, rather than accepting 'we never called it' as grounds for a minor.
Classifies dropping the `verbose` input as a major because removing an input is a breaking change.
Accepts the new `output-file` input with a default as the only item on the list that fits a minor.

Bundles the breaking items into one scheduled v3.0.0 where the forced runtime change is the occasion to delete deprecated inputs, and keeps patching v2 while supported GHES releases cannot run node24.

Rejects 'move the v2 tag as usual' as the delivery mechanism: every fix ships as a new immutable `vX.Y.Z` release because SHA pinners, lockfile users and Dependabot follow new semver tags, never a moved major tag.
Requires release notes to state the full commit SHA and the `uses: corvane/corvane-action@<sha> # vX.Y.Z` line, the form Dependabot updates.
Adds a CI contract check that diffs `action.yml` inputs and outputs against the last release and fails on removal or rename outside a major branch.

evals.prompt: Tallowick sells an infrastructure drift scanner. The CLI `tlw` is Go, binaries on GitHub Releases, exit codes: 0 clean, 2 drift found, 1 runtime error, 3 auth error. Sales keeps saying enterprise customers want us in CI. Plan from the platform meeting: one Docker container action (we already publish an image), inside it fetch `tlw` with `curl -sSL https://get.tallowick.io/install.sh | bash` so customers always get the latest fixes, plus a reusable workflow `tallowick/workflows/.github/workflows/scan.yml@main` so a customer adds two lines and is done. Customer base from the CRM: about 60% GitHub.com, 25% GHES 3.14 to 3.16 behind corporate proxies, a cluster of Windows self-hosted runners at the Terraform-on-Azure accounts, and one large account that runs everything on macOS runners. Seven weeks, 1.5 engineers. Draft the offering.
evals.expected_output: An interview table of assumptions tied to steps, then a design: setup action plus thin task action in two public repos, composite type over the CLI, container and reusable-workflow options deleted with reasons, pinned-and-verified binary download replacing curl-pipe-bash, digest-backed default version with latest only on a signature path, tool-cache, proxy and mirror support, exit-code mapping with a fail-on-drift input, backoff on the vendor API, the rich action named as the starved promotion deferred past the deadline, and the CLI contract handed to the CLI sibling.
expectations: Asks the batched interview questions or writes each assumption in a table with the step it drives (what runs in CI, CI share and runner mix, auth model, existing actions, fork-PR needs, deadline and owner), marking the plan provisional on them.
Deletes the container action option because customers run Windows and macOS runners and container actions run on Linux only.
Deletes the reusable workflow as the product because callers refuse to hand `runs-on` and permissions to a third party and Marketplace cannot list it.
Chooses the default shape: a `setup-tlw` action plus a thin `tlw-action` task action over the same CLI, in two public repos, because Marketplace lists only a root `action.yml`.

Chooses a composite action with all logic in the `tlw` CLI, and names the conditions that would move it to JavaScript: a `post:` cleanup step, native `getIDToken`, annotations at volume, or Windows logic shell cannot carry.
Requires a tested Windows path for every composite step (`shell: pwsh` or Git Bash with its own paths and tools) and `Get-FileHash` for verification on Windows runners.

Rejects `curl | bash` of the installer at runtime; downloads a version-pinned release binary and verifies it against per-version digests committed in the action repo or a signature checked against a pinned signer.

Defaults the CLI version to the newest version the action release ships digests for, so a new CLI version means a new action release, and accepts `latest` only on the signature-verification path resolved from Tallowick's own version endpoint, never the rate-limited GitHub API.
Caches the binary in the runner tool cache (`RUNNER_TOOL_CACHE`) keyed by version and architecture.
Adds a mirror base URL input and a pre-installed binary path for the proxied GHES runners and honours `HTTPS_PROXY`.
Maps exit codes to step results: 1 and 3 (runtime and auth errors) always fail; 2 (drift found) fails by default with a `fail-on-drift: false` input that downgrades it to a warning.
Retries the Tallowick API with backoff because matrix fan-out sends dozens of runs at once.

Names the rich task action (PR comments, annotations, job summary) as the starved option that drift results read inside the pull request would promote, and under the seven-week deadline ships the thin action first with PR output added in a later minor.
Hands the `tlw` flags, `--json` output and exit-code contract to the CLI design sibling as the contract the action is only as stable as.

evals.prompt:
Review our composite action before we publish `brimhaven/brimhaven-action` v1.0.0 on Friday. Security signed off already on the grounds that customers pin us by commit SHA, so what we fetch is covered.

```yaml
name: Brimhaven Scan
description: Runs the Brimhaven dependency scan
inputs:
  api-key:
    required: true
  message:
    description: Text shown in the scan report header
  cli-version:
    default: latest
outputs:
  summary:
    value: ${{ steps.scan.outputs.summary }}
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
    - shell: bash
      run: |
        curl -sSLO https://dl.brimhaven.io/${{ inputs.cli-version }}/bhv
        curl -sSLO https://dl.brimhaven.io/${{ inputs.cli-version }}/bhv.sha256
        sha256sum --check bhv.sha256
        chmod +x bhv
    - id: scan
      shell: bash
      env:
        BHV_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.BRIMHAVEN_TOKEN }}
      run: |
        ./bhv scan --message "${{ inputs.message }}" --token "$BHV_TOKEN" > out.txt
        echo "summary=$(cat out.txt)" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT
        echo "BHV_REPORT=$(cat out.txt)" >> $GITHUB_ENV
```
evals.expected_output: A line-by-line rejection of the security sign-off premise and a corrected action.yml: inputs passed through env and quoted, the secret read from the api-key input and masked, the same-origin checksum replaced by digests committed in the repo with unknown versions refused, latest removed as the default, setup-node pinned by SHA or dropped, outputs written with a random delimiter, the GITHUB_ENV write removed, required inputs validated in code, descriptions and defaults on every optional input, and zizmor and actionlint gates before release.
expectations: Rejects the sign-off premise: a customer's SHA pin on the action pins nothing the action downloads or references at runtime, so nested `uses:` and the fetched binary are uncovered.

Flags `--message "${{ inputs.message }}"` inside `run:` as script injection because the caller decides what flows into `inputs.message`, often `${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}`, and moves the value into `env:` referenced as a quoted `"$MESSAGE"`.
Flags `${{ inputs.cli-version }}` interpolated into the `run:` block as the same injection class and moves it to `env:`.

Flags `${{ secrets.BRIMHAVEN_TOKEN }}` as resolving empty inside a composite action, which has no `secrets` context, and reads the token from the `api-key` input instead, masked with `::add-mask::` before any use.

Rejects the checksum fetched from the same origin as the binary as proving nothing, and replaces it with per-version digests committed in the action repo (a checksums table keyed by version and platform) or a signature verified against a pinned signer identity, refusing any version with no committed digest.
Removes `latest` as the `cli-version` default and defaults to the newest version the action release ships digests for.

Pins `actions/setup-node@v4` by full commit SHA with a version comment, or removes it since the action wraps a native binary, noting that nested `uses:` entries surface as lockfile diffs in customer PRs and should stay few.
Replaces `echo "summary=$(cat out.txt)" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT` with a random-delimiter heredoc (`summary<<EOF_$(openssl rand -hex 8)`) because a newline in the value injects extra outputs.
Removes the `$GITHUB_ENV` write entirely because untrusted text there can set variables such as `NODE_OPTIONS` or `LD_PRELOAD` for every later step.
States that `required: true` is not enforced by the runner and adds in-code validation that fails naming the input, the value received and the expected form.
Adds a `description` and an explicit `default` to every optional input and documents booleans as strict `true`/`false` strings.
Checks that no output embeds the token or any other secret.
Requires zizmor with no finding at medium severity or above and actionlint clean on the action repo and the README example before the v1.0.0 release.

evals.prompt: Ashgrove backend team. We're adding OIDC to `ashgrove/deploy-action` so customers stop pasting API keys into secrets. Design doc so far: the action requests the GitHub ID token with the default audience and posts it to `/v1/token/exchange`; we verify the JWT signature against GitHub's JWKS, check `iss == https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com` and that `aud` is present, and that counts as authenticated. The customer then links an Ashgrove project in our UI by typing a pattern like `repo:their-org/their-repo:*` which we match against `sub`. If the exchange fails, the action quietly falls back to the `api-key` input, and if that's empty too it runs in anonymous read-only mode so nobody's pipeline breaks. Current v2 has `api-key` as a required input, so the OIDC path will go out as v3. Our two biggest accounts are on GHES 3.15. Tear this apart.
evals.expected_output: A rewritten auth design: vendor-specific audience, per-claim trust binding on numeric repository and owner IDs plus ref or environment, sub wildcard rejected with the immutable sub format explained, silent fallback and anonymous mode replaced by named failures, an auth input with auto/oidc/key semantics shipped as a v2 minor, token lifetime and masking rules, JWKS and time-claim checks, the permissions block documented, GHES handled through a registered issuer or key-only, a binding UI that shows claims and logs rejections, and fork PRs handled without pull_request_target.
expectations: Rejects the default audience: the action requests a vendor-specific audience and the backend rejects a blank or default `aud`, because a default audience accepts tokens minted for other services.
States that issuer plus audience alone is never enough, because the issuer is shared by every GitHub customer, so at least one customer trust binding must match before the exchange succeeds.

Replaces `sub` string matching with per-claim matching on `repository_owner_id` (required) and `repository_id` (recommended), numeric and never reassigned, plus one of `ref`, `environment` or `job_workflow_ref`.

Rejects the `repo:their-org/their-repo:*` wildcard, explains the immutable `sub` format with numeric IDs (`repo:octo-org@123456/octo-repo@456789:ref:...`) that is default for repositories created, renamed or transferred after 2026-07-15, and notes organizations can customize the `sub` template so string matching is fragile.
Rejects the silent fallback to `api-key` and the anonymous read-only mode: an OIDC failure must fail the step with a named error because a silent fallback hides a broken trust setup.

Specifies an `auth` input with values `auto`, `oidc` and `key` (default `auto`), where an empty key selects OIDC, a missing `ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL` fails naming both causes (api-key empty and the job lacks `id-token: write`) because a missing secret also arrives empty, and the chosen mode is logged.
States OIDC ships as a v2 minor by making `api-key` optional with `auth` defaulting to `auto`, since old workflows that set the key behave the same, rather than cutting v3.
Requires the exchanged Ashgrove token to live minutes, carry only the binding's scopes, be logged with the claims that matched, and be masked before any log line.
Checks `exp`, `nbf` and `iat` within a small clock skew, and caches JWKS keys with a refetch on an unknown `kid`.
Documents the minimum `permissions:` block (`id-token: write`, `contents: read`) in the README snippet.

Handles GHES 3.15 explicitly: its tokens come from `https://<host>/_services/token`, usually unreachable from a SaaS backend, so support a customer-registered issuer whose JWKS is exposed through an allowlist, or an uploaded JWKS with a rotation procedure, or document GHES as key-only.
Specifies that the binding UI shows the exact claim values a sample token would need and offers a test-with-a-real-run that logs the last rejected token's claims.

States fork `pull_request` runs receive no secrets and no `id-token: write`, so the action runs tokenless read-only where the product allows it or exits naming the limitation, and never tells customers to switch to `pull_request_target`.
Offers an optional `event_name` binding so a customer can refuse tokens from `pull_request_target` runs.

evals.prompt: Fennwater's `fennwater/coverage-action` posts a coverage-diff comment on pull requests. Open-source maintainers keep complaining it does nothing on PRs from forks. Our support macro currently tells them to switch the trigger to `pull_request_target` and check out `${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` so the token is available. One of our engineers proposed instead: on `pull_request` the action writes the coverage JSON plus the PR number into an artifact, then a `workflow_run` job downloads it, reads the PR number and posts the comment with `contents: write`. Each push creates a new comment, we're fine with that. Also, the comment currently lists every uncovered file path from the repo's source tree, which customers like. Which way do we go, and write the docs page we should publish.
evals.expected_output: The pull_request_target macro withdrawn, fork behaviour defined as tokenless or a named exit, the two-workflow split adopted with the PR resolved from head_sha through the commits-to-pulls API instead of the artifact, the artifact validated as data and downloaded by run ID, fork code never executed, permissions narrowed to actions: read and pull-requests: write, the comment upserted by hidden marker filtered to the token's own identity and capped at the body limit, file paths replaced by counts in public repositories, PR text escaped, and the example carrying only a line-scoped zizmor ignore.
expectations: Withdraws the `pull_request_target` support macro: it runs with base-repository secrets against fork code, and GitHub blocks it by default in public repositories from 2026-12-02.

States that fork `pull_request` runs get a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN`, no secrets and no OIDC token, and makes the action either run in a tokenless read-only mode or exit with a message naming the limitation.
Adopts the two-workflow split, with the `pull_request` workflow running the action without credentials and uploading the result as an artifact.
Rejects reading the PR number from the artifact because a PR number inside the artifact is attacker-controlled.

Resolves the PR from `workflow_run.head_sha` through `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits/{sha}/pulls` and requires that PR's head SHA to equal it, noting `workflow_run.pull_requests` is empty for fork PRs.
Downloads the artifact by run ID and validates it as data (schema, size) before anything reads it.
Makes the `workflow_run` workflow name the first workflow in `workflows:`, run only on `conclusion == 'success'`, and never check out or execute fork code.
Scopes the second workflow to `actions: read` plus `pull-requests: write` and rejects `contents: write`.

Replaces the comment-per-push with an upsert: one comment per action and job, found by a hidden marker such as `<!-- fennwater-action:coverage -->` and filtered to comments authored by the token's own identity, because anyone can post the marker.
Truncates the comment body at GitHub's 65,536-character cap and links to the job summary for the full result.
Removes the uncovered-file-path list from comments in public repositories: show counts and identifiers and link the details behind vendor login, because the comment is public.
Escapes any text taken from the PR (titles, file names) before it goes into the Markdown body.
Keeps the basic README example free of zizmor findings and lets the fork-split example carry only a line-scoped, commented ignore for its `workflow_run` trigger.

evals.prompt: Sorrelby maintainer here, two things on `sorrelby/setup-sorrel`. (1) We turned on immutable releases last month because security asked for it. Now our release script, which runs `git tag -f v1 <sha> && git push -f --tags` with the release bot's PAT, fails on the v1 push. We had published a `v1` GitHub release back in 2024 because it shows up nicely on the Marketplace page. Simplest fix seems to be turning immutable releases back off. (2) Last Tuesday that same bot PAT turned up in a Slack export someone shared externally. We revoked it, minted a new one, and checked that the v1 and v2 tags still point where we expected. Are we done?
evals.expected_output: Immutable releases kept on with the real cause explained (v1 carries a release), major tags made release-free, the push narrowed to one tag ref, the bot PAT replaced by a GitHub App token from a protected release environment, a tag ruleset and 2FA, and the leak handled with the full runbook: rotate every write credential rather than the one PAT, freeze releases, audit every tag against the release record and signed tags, publish an advisory and notify customers if any target changed, sign tags going forward, and build, attest and publish through the release workflow.
expectations: Keeps immutable releases on and explains the failure: the `v1` tag carries a GitHub release, so it cannot move; major tags must be plain release-free Git tags and only `vX.Y.Z` tags carry releases.
Rejects turning immutable releases off as the fix.
Replaces `git push -f --tags` with a push of the single moved tag as `refs/tags/v1`, because `--tags` pushes every local tag.
Removes the release from `v1` (recreating it as a plain tag at the released commit) and points Marketplace consumers at the `vX.Y.Z` releases.
Replaces the bot PAT with a short-lived GitHub App token used by a release workflow running in a protected environment with required reviewers.
Protects `v*` tags with a ruleset that only the release workflow's GitHub App can bypass, requires 2FA, and shortens the write-access list.

Treats the leaked PAT as a compromised-credential incident and revokes and rotates every credential with write access (maintainer sessions, other PATs, App keys, deploy keys), not only the leaked PAT, because incomplete rotation re-opened the door in the 2026 trivy-action incident.
Freezes releases and restricts the tag ruleset to nobody while the audit runs.
Compares every tag's target against the release record and signed tags, not only `v1` and `v2`, because past incidents repointed every tag at once.

Publishes a GitHub security advisory with affected tags, exposure window, known-good SHAs and the instruction to rotate any secret exposed to the action if any tag target changed, and notifies customers through Sorrelby's own channels and the `User-Agent` list of repositories that ran affected versions.
Signs release tags and commits from now on, noting forged tags in past incidents were unsigned with impossible parent dates.
Moves the release to the workflow sequence: build binaries in CI, attest them, create a draft `vX.Y.Z` release, attach assets, publish, then move `vX` from the same job.
Scopes `GITHUB_TOKEN` per job from `permissions: {}` and keeps the action's own CI off `pull_request_target`, `workflow_run` over fork code and `issue_comment` triggers.

evals.prompt: Quillstone, API linting SaaS. A contractor who left two years ago wrote `jmbarros-dev/quillstone-lint-action`; about 380 repos use it, mostly `@v2`, a few on `@v3` which was a half-finished rewrite with renamed inputs. He's happy to transfer the repo to us. Our plan: accept the transfer into my personal org `kaspar-tools` for now because the company org isn't set up for Marketplace yet, delete the v3 tags since that contract is wrong, re-cut v3 with our input names, lean on a big Marketplace listing push with a launch post for adoption, and tell GHES customers to download the repo zip and vendor it into their instance. For GHES OIDC we'll reuse the same token exchange we built for github.com. Thoughts?
evals.expected_output: The transfer accepted with migration messaging because the redirect can die, the org chosen once because a later transfer drops the verified badge, inherited tags audited and v3 declared unsupported instead of deleted, Quillstone's contract shipped as v4 rather than a reused v3, a migration guide, Marketplace reframed as a trust surface with adoption driven by the docs quickstart snippet and a SHA-pinned README example, the verified creator badge requested through partnerships, GHES reached through GitHub Connect or actions-sync, GHES OIDC handled through a registered issuer or key-only, and immutable releases enabled before the first tag.
expectations: Accepts the transfer path (maintainer agrees, contract close) but publishes the new `uses:` path and asks users to migrate, because the redirect dies if anyone recreates `jmbarros-dev/quillstone-lint-action`.

Rejects transferring into the personal org `kaspar-tools` first: choose the final org and repo name once, because a later transfer keeps the redirect but drops the Marketplace verified badge unless the new owner is verified.
Rejects deleting the v3 tags: declare pre-transfer tags unsupported without deleting them, because deleting a tag breaks every pinned workflow at once.
Rejects re-cutting v3 with different input names: never reuse a version number the community action already shipped with a different contract, so Quillstone's contract ships as v4.
Audits every inherited tag against the maintainer's history before the first release under the new owner.
Publishes a migration guide mapping the old v2 and v3 inputs to the new names.
Reframes the Marketplace push: the listing is unreviewed and a trust surface, adoption follows Quillstone's own docs and onboarding snippets, so the same snippet goes into the docs quickstart.

Opens the README with a copy-paste workflow: the SHA-pinned `uses:` line with its version comment, the `permissions:` block, the OIDC setup, every input with default, every output, and the minimum runner and GHES versions.
Requests the verified creator badge through GitHub partnerships, noting enterprise allowlists key on it more than on listing rank.
Keeps one `action.yml` at the root of the public repo with a unique `name`, short `description`, `branding` icon and color, and one primary category.
Replaces 'download the zip and vendor it' with GitHub Connect when the GHES admin enables it, otherwise `actions-sync` into the instance.

Rejects reusing the github.com token exchange unchanged for GHES: GHES signs OIDC tokens with its own issuer on a network the backend usually cannot reach, so support a customer-registered issuer or uploaded JWKS, or document GHES as key-only.
Enables immutable releases on the repository before the first public tag under Quillstone's ownership.

evals.prompt: Marrowfield's `mfd` CLI ships as a glibc-linked Linux binary plus Windows and macOS builds. Our GitHub Action is live. Paying-customer CI breakdown from last quarter's survey: GitHub 68%, GitLab 19%, Azure DevOps 7%, CircleCI 3%, Bitbucket 2%, Jenkins 1%. The platform PM wants native integrations for all six this quarter because CircleCI and Jenkins are huge in the market, with each integration owning its own logic so the teams can iterate independently. Drafts so far: a GitLab component with `spec: inputs: {}` (inputs come later), a CircleCI orb we'd publish as `mfd/mfd@dev:latest` so we can hotfix in place, an Azure DevOps task declaring the `Node20` handler, and a Bitbucket pipe where we re-push the `1.0.0` image tag whenever we fix a bug. One engineer for one quarter. Prioritize and correct.
evals.expected_output: Ports ranked by paying-customer share with snippets everywhere and native packages only for GitLab and possibly Azure DevOps, Jenkins last, every port a thin wrapper over the same CLI with one input schema, and each draft corrected: no empty inputs key and the templates layout for GitLab, immutable production orb versions instead of dev labels, the right Azure handler keys and agent floor, publish-once Bitbucket tags, per-port semver with a compatibility table, snippets with pinned verified downloads, full history and a glibc base image, and the same versioned User-Agent from each port.
expectations: Ranks ports by the share of paying customers on each CI, not by platform popularity, rejecting the 'CircleCI and Jenkins are huge' argument.
Prescribes the default: documented, tested CLI snippets for every CI plus a native package only for the one or two CI systems holding most non-GitHub customers (GitLab, possibly Azure DevOps).
Budgets Jenkins last or not at all, stating a Jenkins plugin is a Maven-versioned update-center release justified only by real enterprise revenue on Jenkins.
Rejects per-integration independent logic: every port stays a thin wrapper over the same `mfd` CLI with the same input names, because a port that reimplements logic drifts within a few releases.
Keeps one input schema and generates or checks each manifest (`action.yml`, component `spec:inputs`, orb parameters, `pipe.yml` variables, `task.json` inputs) against it.

Fixes the GitLab component: omit `inputs:` under `spec:` while there are none because an empty `inputs:` key fails release creation, and lays out the project with `README.md` plus a top-level `templates/` directory.

Notes GitLab catalog publishing needs a semantic-version release, that `~latest` skips pre-releases but can include breaking changes, and that turning off the catalog toggle destroys catalog metadata.

Rejects `dev:latest` for customers: `dev:<label>` orb versions are mutable and expire after 90 days, while production versions `<namespace>/<orb>@1.2.3` are immutable and cannot be deleted, so a bad release is fixed only by a newer one.
Chooses the CircleCI namespace once because renaming needs CircleCI support, and documents that partner orbs need customers to allow uncertified orbs in their organization settings.

Corrects the Azure DevOps handler: no `Node20` key exists; declare both `Node20_1` and `Node24` during the transition, `Node24` needs `minimumAgentVersion` 4.265.1, and test on the oldest supported Windows Server agent.
Rejects re-pushing the Bitbucket `1.0.0` tag: image tags are mutable on the registry, so publish each version once and never re-push a tag.
Gives each port its own semver bumped by its own contract and publishes one compatibility table mapping each port version to the CLI version range it installs.

Makes every snippet download a pinned CLI version with checksum verification, set full Git history where the CLI needs it (`fetch-depth: 0` on GitHub, `GIT_DEPTH: 0` on GitLab), and use a glibc base image because `mfd` is not built for musl.
Sends the same versioned `User-Agent` with the CI name from every port and tests auth claims, output passing and secret masking per port, the three places drift concentrates.

evals.prompt: Oxleaf here. `oxleaf/oxleaf-action` is JavaScript on node20 with majors v1 (2023, still a few users), v2, and v3 current at 3.3.1. Since GitHub removed node20 last month our v3 runs show the runtime warning. Plan: ship `runs.using: node24` in v3.4.0 next week and move the v3 tag; delete the v1 tags since it's ancient and nobody should be on it; keep the deprecated `token` input (replaced by `api-key` in v3.1) because removing it is a hassle. For the board deck we want usage numbers: Marketplace installs, the 'Used by' dependents count, and a GitHub code search for `uses: oxleaf/oxleaf-action@`. Our README says macOS and ARM self-hosted runners are supported and we'll keep that line. Sanity check.
evals.expected_output: node24 moved into a v4.0.0 major that also deletes the deprecated token input once the deprecated-input flag count says so, v3 kept patched on node20 for GHES, v1 retired by announcement and a last warning patch with its tags left in place, delivery through vX.Y.Z releases rather than a moved tag, the proposed usage numbers replaced by token-exchange counts deduplicated by run_id and User-Agent telemetry with the four tracked metrics, the README runner claim corrected for Node 24 limits, the self-hosted oldest-runner matrix job, ESM dist with check-dist, and v4 tested on node24 rather than relying on the forced run.
expectations: Classifies `runs.using: node24` as a major (v4.0.0), not a v3.4.0 minor, because it raises the minimum runner and breaks GHES and old self-hosted runners.
Uses the forced runtime major to delete the deprecated `token` input, choosing the removal major from the count of runs still setting it reported by the deprecated-input header flag.
Keeps patching v3 on node20 while supported GHES releases cannot run node24.
Rejects deleting the v1 tags: retire a major by announcing it, warning from its last patch release, and leaving its tags in place, because deleting a tag breaks every pinned workflow at once.
Rejects 'move the v3 tag' as the delivery: ships a `vX.Y.Z` release so SHA pinners, lockfile users and Dependabot receive it.
Rejects Marketplace installs, the dependents count and code search as usage numbers: they are public signals, not usage.
Counts OIDC-authenticated runs from token exchanges deduplicated by `run_id`, using server-validated `repository_id` and `repository_owner_id` claims.
Measures key-auth runs and version skew through the versioned `User-Agent` (`oxleaf-action/3.3.1 (github-actions; Linux-X64)`) with a header flag whenever a deprecated input is set.
Reports to the board: weekly active repositories by CI and version, share of runs on supported majors, first-run failure rate by error class, and support tickets per release.
Corrects the README support claim because Node 24 does not run on macOS 13.4 and earlier or on ARM32 self-hosted runners, so the minimum runner and OS line changes with the major.
Runs one integration job on a self-hosted runner pinned to the oldest supported runner version before release, because hosted runners hide the runtime-floor break.
Rebuilds and commits `dist/` bundled as ESM and adds check-dist (`git diff --ignore-space-at-eol --text dist/`) to the release gates.
Notes that actions still declaring node20 after removal run on node24 with a job warning, untested by their authors, so v4 is tested on node24 rather than left to the forced run.
